purpose: Computes the nth Fibonacci number using direct recursion
explanation: The function returns 0 for n=0, 1 for n=1, and the sum of the previous two values otherwise. The recursive structure mirrors the mathematical definition exactly. Unfortunately it has exponential O(2^n) time because the same subproblems are recomputed across many branches: fib(35) makes over 18 million calls. Useful as a teaching example, not as production code; memoize it (see CE-002) or iterate (CE-003).
walkthrough: Line 1 declares the function with one int parameter. Line 2 is the base case: if n is 0 or 1, return n directly (fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1). Line 3 is the recursive case: split into two subproblems and add. The call tree is a binary tree of depth n with no sharing, hence the exponential blowup.

purpose: Memoizes the recursive Fibonacci so each n is computed once
explanation: Same recursion as CE-001 but wrapped in `@lru_cache`, which transparently caches return values keyed on arguments. The first call for any n computes and stores the result; subsequent calls hit the cache. Time goes from O(2^n) to O(n); space is O(n) for the cache. fib(1000) is now instant.
walkthrough: Line 1 imports lru_cache. Line 3 applies it as a decorator with no size limit. Inside fib the body is identical to CE-001, but lru_cache intercepts each call: if (n,) is already in its dict, return the cached value; else compute, store, return.

purpose: Computes Fibonacci iteratively in constant space
explanation: Tracks two consecutive Fibonacci values and advances by tuple-unpacking on each iteration. Time is O(n), space is O(1) (just the two locals). For most production uses this is the right form: no stack depth, no cache memory.
walkthrough: Line 2 initialises a=0 (fib of 0) and b=1 (fib of 1). The loop runs n times. Line 4 simultaneously sets the new a to the old b and the new b to a+b, advancing by one Fibonacci step. After n iterations a is fib(n).

purpose: Returns the index of `target` in a sorted array, or -1 if absent
explanation: Classic O(log n) divide-and-conquer search. At each step it inspects the middle element, returning if it matches; otherwise narrowing the search to the half that could contain the target. Requires the input to be sorted. The standard library has bisect_left/bisect_right which solve the related insertion-point problem.
walkthrough: lo and hi maintain an inclusive search interval [lo, hi]. The loop runs while there's at least one element in the interval. mid is the middle index (integer division). On match, return. On too-small middle, slide lo past mid. On too-large middle, slide hi before mid. If the loop exits the target wasn't found.

purpose: Sorts a slice of ints in place using a three-way partition quicksort
explanation: Recursively partitions the slice around a pivot (here the middle element). Three buckets — less, equal, greater — handle duplicates cleanly without infinite recursion. After sorting the less and greater buckets, the result is concatenated and copied back into the original slice. Average time O(n log n), worst case O(n^2) when the pivot consistently splits unevenly.
walkthrough: Base case: arrays of length 0 or 1 are already sorted. Pick a pivot. Walk the input once, dropping each element into one of the three buckets. Recurse on less and greater (equal is already sorted). Concatenate and copy the result back into the input slice.

purpose: Breadth-first traversal of a graph from a start node
explanation: Maintains a queue of nodes to visit and a set of nodes already seen. Each iteration pops the front, records it, and enqueues all unvisited neighbours. The result is the visit order, which corresponds to shortest-path distance in unweighted graphs. deque gives O(1) popleft; using a list would be O(n) per pop.
walkthrough: Initialise visited with the start (so we don't revisit). Initialise the queue with the start. Loop while the queue isn't empty: pop the front, append to order, look at each neighbour; if it's new, mark it visited and enqueue it. The visited check before enqueue prevents duplicate work and infinite loops on cyclic graphs.

purpose: Sorts a Vec<i32> by recursive merge sort
explanation: Divides the input in half, recursively sorts each half, then merges the two sorted halves with a two-pointer scan. O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space. Stable: equal elements keep their relative order because the comparison uses `<=`. The Vec::with_capacity hint avoids repeated reallocation.
walkthrough: Base case: 0 or 1 element is already sorted. Compute the midpoint, recurse on each half (each half is owned via to_vec). Merge: walk both halves with index pointers, taking the smaller front element each step. extend_from_slice appends whatever remains in the longer half.

purpose: Depth-first traversal of a graph using a recursive helper
explanation: Recursively visits each node, marking it as seen on entry to prevent cycles. The traversal order is preorder: a node is recorded before its children. The optional-chaining-with-default `graph[node] ?? []` handles missing keys gracefully. For deep graphs the call stack is the bottleneck; iterative DFS with an explicit stack avoids stack overflow for very deep graphs.
walkthrough: visit returns immediately if the node was already visited. Otherwise it marks it, records the order, and recurses into each neighbour. The outer function kicks off the traversal at start and returns the order list.

purpose: Returns the k largest values from an iterable
explanation: heapq.nlargest uses a min-heap of size k, walking the input once. Time complexity O(n log k), space O(k). Beats sorting (O(n log n)) when k is small, e.g. top 10 of a million values. Symmetric counterpart heapq.nsmallest exists. Both accept a `key=` parameter for custom ordering.
walkthrough: The implementation maintains a min-heap of the k largest values seen so far. Each input element is compared against the heap minimum: if it's larger, the minimum is popped and the new value is pushed. The result is sorted descending.

purpose: Reverses a slice of ints in place
explanation: Two pointers, one at each end, walk toward the middle swapping elements. The loop condition i < j stops at the midpoint (no need to swap the middle element with itself). O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space, in-place. Generic: with Go 1.18+ the same shape works for any comparable element type.
walkthrough: i starts at 0, j at the last index. Each iteration swaps s[i] and s[j], then advances i and retreats j. The loop exits when they meet or cross.

purpose: A simple singly-linked list with an O(n) append
explanation: Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node (or None for the tail). Append walks to the end and links the new node. O(n) per append because we don't track the tail; for many appends, keep a tail pointer to make append O(1). For modern Python a deque from collections is usually faster than a hand-written linked list.
walkthrough: Node stores value and next. append handles two cases: empty list (return the new node as the new head) and non-empty list (walk to the last node, attach the new one to its next, return the unchanged head).

purpose: Inserts a value into a binary search tree
explanation: Recursively descends until it finds a null pointer, then attaches a fresh leaf. Equal values are ignored (a set, not a multiset). For balanced trees the operation is O(log n); for adversarial input that produces a degenerate left- or right-only chain, it's O(n). Self-balancing variants (AVL, red-black) keep the worst case at O(log n).
walkthrough: Null root: create and return a new leaf. Smaller value: recurse into the left subtree, reattaching whatever it returns. Larger value: same on the right. Equal value: do nothing. Always return root so the parent's pointer can be updated.

purpose: A FIFO queue implemented with two stacks
explanation: Enqueue pushes onto in_stack. Dequeue pops from out_stack, refilling out_stack from in_stack (in reversed order) when empty. Each element is moved at most twice across both stacks, so the amortised cost of any single operation is O(1) even though one dequeue may do O(n) work. Classic interview problem.
walkthrough: in_stack holds newly-enqueued elements in arrival order. out_stack holds elements ready to leave (oldest on top). enqueue is trivial. dequeue: if out_stack is empty, drain in_stack into it (which reverses order so the oldest is on top), then pop.

purpose: Least-Recently-Used cache with O(1) get and put
explanation: OrderedDict maintains insertion order and supports O(1) move_to_end. On access, move the key to the back (most-recently-used). On insert past capacity, popitem(last=False) drops the front (least-recently-used). All operations are O(1). For high-throughput needs, functools.lru_cache wraps function calls; for explicit caching this pattern works directly.
walkthrough: get: if missing return -1, else move the key to the end (refresh recency) and return the value. put: if existing, refresh; then write; if over capacity, evict the front.

purpose: An immutable linked-list node with a structural push (returns a new head)
explanation: Each node stores its value plus an optional boxed next, which is how Rust handles recursive data types (Box gives heap indirection so the size is known at compile time). push consumes self and returns a new node whose next is the previous head. Functional style: nothing is mutated. For mutable operations use Rc<RefCell<Node>> or unsafe raw pointers.
walkthrough: Node holds a value and an Option<Box<Node>>; None means end of list. push takes ownership of the current node and returns a new one whose next is Some(Box::new(self)). Each push allocates one Box on the heap.

purpose: Returns the n most frequent words in a text and their counts
explanation: Counter is a dict subclass that counts hashable items. Constructed from any iterable, it tallies frequencies in O(n). most_common(n) returns the top n as (item, count) tuples sorted descending. Useful for word frequency analysis, n-gram statistics, log analysis, anything frequency-based.
walkthrough: Lowercase and split the text into words. Pass the list to Counter, which builds a {word: count} mapping internally. most_common(n) returns the top-n by count, ties broken by insertion order.

purpose: Groups words by their first letter
explanation: defaultdict(list) creates an empty list automatically when a missing key is accessed, eliminating the if-not-in-dict-init-it boilerplate. Convert back to a regular dict at the end to avoid surprises (the defaultdict creates entries on read, not just write). Common pattern for grouping, bucketing, indexing.
walkthrough: defaultdict's argument is a factory called on missing keys (here list). The loop accesses groups[word[0]]; if that key doesn't exist, defaultdict creates groups[word[0]] = [] and returns it. Then append. dict(groups) at the end snapshots the populated keys.

snippet:
with open('data.csv') as f:
    next(f)  # skip header
    for line in f:
        cols = line.strip().split(',')
        process(cols)
purpose: Streams a CSV line by line, skipping the header
explanation: Opens the file inside a `with` block so it closes automatically. next(f) consumes the first line (the header). The loop iterates lazily, one line at a time, so memory usage is constant regardless of file size. .strip() removes the trailing newline; split(',') tokenizes. For real CSVs with quoted fields use the csv module; this is fine for simple data.
walkthrough: with opens and binds f. next(f) reads and discards the first line. The for loop reads remaining lines lazily. Each iteration trims whitespace and splits on commas. The with block closes f on exit, even if process() raises.

snippet:
from contextlib import contextmanager
import time

@contextmanager
def timed(label):
    t0 = time.time()
    yield
    print(f'{label}: {time.time() - t0:.3f}s')
purpose: A context manager that prints elapsed time
explanation: @contextmanager turns a generator into a context manager. Code before yield runs on __enter__; code after runs on __exit__. Use as `with timed('block name'): do_work()` and the elapsed time prints at the end. Production-quality variant should use try/finally so the timing prints even if the block raises.
walkthrough: The decorator turns the generator into a class with __enter__/__exit__. yield returns control to the with-body. After the body, execution resumes here. If you wrap yield in try/finally, the elapsed-time print runs even on exception.

purpose: Uses defer to ensure the file is closed even on early return
explanation: defer schedules a call to run when the surrounding function returns, regardless of how. The pattern guarantees cleanup without nesting or repeated cleanup code at every return path. defer arguments are evaluated immediately but the call runs later. Multiple defers stack in LIFO order. Idiomatic Go for resource cleanup (files, mutex unlock, http response body close).
walkthrough: Open the file, check the error. The defer line schedules f.Close() for after process returns. The body can return early, panic, or complete normally; in each case Close() runs.

purpose: Parses a string to int and returns it doubled, propagating errors with `?`
explanation: Rust's `?` operator unwraps a Result: if Ok, gives the inner value; if Err, returns it from the enclosing function (after applying any From conversions). map_err here converts the parse error type to String first so it matches the function's return type. The pattern produces clean error-propagation chains without manual match statements. Equivalent to early-return on Err.
walkthrough: trim() removes whitespace, parse() attempts to make an i32 returning Result. map_err converts the parse error to String. The ? returns the error from parse_int if any, else unwraps to the int. Multiply by 2 and wrap in Ok.

snippet: evens_squared = [x * x for x in range(20) if x % 2 == 0]
purpose: Builds a list of squares of even numbers in 0..19
explanation: List comprehension: a single expression that combines a loop, a filter, and a transformation. Equivalent to a 4-line for loop that appends to an initially-empty list. More than just terser: the comprehension runs the loop in C inside the CPython interpreter, so it's noticeably faster than the equivalent explicit loop. Generator expression `(x*x for ...)` is the lazy variant.
walkthrough: range(20) yields 0..19. The `if x % 2 == 0` filter keeps only even values. The expression `x * x` transforms each kept value. The brackets collect into a list. Result: [0, 4, 16, 36, 64, 100, 144, 196, 256, 324].

snippet: const city = user?.address?.city ?? 'unknown';
purpose: Reads a deeply-nested field with safe defaults
explanation: Optional chaining `?.` returns undefined if the left side is null/undefined instead of throwing. Nullish coalescing `??` returns the right side if the left is null/undefined (NOT for empty string or 0). Together they replace the older `user && user.address && user.address.city || 'unknown'` pattern, which was wrong for falsy-but-non-null values. Both operators landed in ES2020.
walkthrough: user?.address: returns user.address if user is non-null, else undefined. Then ?.city: returns .city if address exists, else undefined. Then ?? 'unknown': substitutes 'unknown' if the result is null or undefined.

purpose: Classifies an integer into named buckets using pattern matching
explanation: Rust's match is exhaustive: the compiler verifies every possible value is handled (the trailing _ catch-all here ensures it). Patterns can match literals (0), inclusive ranges (1..=9), and have guards (`_ if n < 0`). Order matters: first matching arm wins. More expressive than a chain of if/else if/else and statically checked for completeness.
walkthrough: Each arm is `pattern => expression`. The compiler checks that the patterns collectively cover every i32. Guards (`if n < 0`) further refine. The function returns the string of the first matching arm.

purpose: A simple memoization decorator
explanation: memoize is a higher-order function: it takes a function and returns a wrapped version. The wrapper holds a closure over `cache`, which persists between calls. functools.wraps copies the original function's name and docstring onto wrapper so introspection still works. functools.lru_cache is the production version with size limits and proper handling of unhashable arguments.
walkthrough: memoize: receives fn, defines a closure over cache, returns wrapper. wrapper: checks args in cache; if missing, computes fn(*args) and stores; returns the cached value. @memoize on slow rebinds the name `slow` to the wrapped version.

purpose: Producer goroutine sending values, consumer ranging until close
explanation: Buffered channel of size 3: sends block only when the buffer is full. The goroutine sends 0..4 then closes. The for-range loop on a channel reads values until close. close + range is the canonical pattern for a finite producer; range without close on an unbuffered or unclosed channel deadlocks when the producer stops. Concurrent communication via channels rather than shared memory is Go's defining concurrency model.
walkthrough: make(chan int, 3) creates a buffered channel. The goroutine sends 5 values then closes. The main loop reads each value as it arrives; range exits when the channel is closed AND drained.

purpose: Singleton via a class decorator (one instance per decorated class)
explanation: The decorator replaces the class with a callable that lazily constructs the single instance on first call and returns the same instance on subsequent calls. Pythonic: avoids the metaclass machinery of textbook singletons. Caveat: arguments after the first call are silently ignored, so the API is a bit lying. For most config-style cases that's fine; for stricter behaviour, raise on differing args.
walkthrough: singleton wraps cls in get_instance. get_instance keeps an instances dict keyed by class (so the same decorator can decorate multiple classes). First call: construct, store, return. Subsequent calls: return the stored instance.

purpose: Factory that constructs animals by string tag, with full type safety
explanation: TypeScript's union string literal types ('dog' | 'cat') give the caller a closed set of valid inputs that the type checker verifies. The switch is exhaustive: TypeScript will warn if you add a case to the union without handling it. The factory pattern centralises object creation, decoupling callers from constructor details. Common in DI frameworks and plugin systems.
walkthrough: Animal interface declares speak. Dog and Cat implement it. animalFactory takes a literal-typed kind, switches on it, returns the appropriate concrete instance typed as the abstract Animal.

purpose: Observer pattern: subscribers receive events the publisher emits
explanation: Subject keeps a list of callbacks. Subscribers register, the publisher iterates and calls each on notify. Loose coupling: the publisher doesn't know who's listening; subscribers don't know about each other. Caveats not shown: thread safety on the observer list, error isolation per callback, unsubscribe support. Frameworks (RxPy, asyncio events, signals/slots in Qt) productionise this.
walkthrough: Subject's _observers is a list of callables. subscribe appends. notify iterates and invokes each. The lambda subscriber prints. After s.notify('hello') the lambda runs once and prints 'got hello'.

purpose: Builder pattern for an immutable Pizza with fluent topping construction
explanation: The static inner Builder accumulates state via methods returning `this`, then build() constructs the immutable Pizza. The outer Pizza has a private constructor so the only way to create one is through the builder. Standard Java pattern for objects with many optional parameters or invariants that need validation at build time. Effective Java item 2 explains why this beats telescoping constructors.
walkthrough: Pizza's constructor is private. Builder collects toppings in its own list with chainable topping() calls. build() passes the builder into Pizza's private constructor, which copies the list. The result is an immutable Pizza.

purpose: Strategy pattern via a dispatch dict
explanation: Maps operation names to callables. Selecting the strategy is a dict lookup. Adding a new operation is one dict entry; no class hierarchy needed. Pythonic alternative to the OO Strategy pattern with abstract base + concrete subclasses. Tradeoff: callers can pass arbitrary strings; consider a literal-typed enum or KeyError handling for production.
walkthrough: OPS keys are strategy names; values are the implementing callables. calc looks up the strategy by name and invokes it with the arguments. Adding 'div' is one line.

purpose: Decorator factory that retries a flaky function on exception
explanation: Three nesting levels: retry(times) returns a decorator parameterised on times; the decorator wraps a function; the wrapper retries on exception. Production retry should add backoff (exponential or jittered), per-exception filtering (don't retry on programmer errors), and a max-time budget. tenacity is the standard library for retries in Python.
walkthrough: retry(times) is a function call returning a decorator. The decorator wraps fn in wrapper. wrapper tries up to `times` calls; on exception, stores it and continues; if all attempts failed, re-raises the last error.

purpose: Polymorphic dispatch through trait objects
explanation: `dyn Animal` is a trait object: a fat pointer carrying a data pointer plus a vtable for method dispatch. Box stores the concrete type on the heap. Vec<Box<dyn Animal>> holds heterogeneous animals. The for loop calls speak() through dynamic dispatch. Alternative: enums of all known types (closed set, monomorphised), or generics over T: Animal (closed at compile time, no vtable).
walkthrough: Each impl block adds a speak method. Box::new(Dog) puts a Dog on the heap and returns a smart pointer. Vec stores Box<dyn Animal> (trait objects). The loop borrows each element and calls speak via the vtable.

snippet:
import asyncio
import aiohttp

async def fetch(session, url):
    async with session.get(url) as r:
        return await r.text()

async def main(urls):
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        return await asyncio.gather(
            *(fetch(session, u) for u in urls)
        )

pages = asyncio.run(main(['https://a', 'https://b']))
purpose: Concurrently fetches a list of URLs
explanation: asyncio.gather runs many coroutines concurrently and waits for all. Sharing a single ClientSession reuses connections (connection pooling). Total wall time is roughly the slowest single fetch, not the sum. Compare with threading: asyncio is one OS thread doing async I/O; threading would be many OS threads. For pure I/O-bound work asyncio is more efficient at high concurrency.
walkthrough: fetch is a coroutine that opens a request and reads the body. main creates a session, builds N fetch coroutines, gathers them into one awaitable. asyncio.run executes the event loop until main completes.

snippet:
import os
import tempfile

def atomic_write(path, data):
    dir_ = os.path.dirname(path) or '.'
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=dir_)
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, 'w') as f:
            f.write(data)
        os.replace(tmp, path)
    except Exception:
        os.unlink(tmp)
        raise
purpose: Atomic file write: a reader sees either the old file or the new, never partial
explanation: Writes to a temp file in the same directory (so os.replace works across the same filesystem), then atomically renames over the destination. os.replace on POSIX is rename(2), which is atomic. The try/except removes the temp on any failure. Standard pattern for config files, caches, anywhere a partial write would corrupt downstream readers. shutil.move does NOT guarantee atomicity across filesystems.
walkthrough: mkstemp creates a unique temp file in the destination directory. Write into it via fdopen. os.replace atomically moves the temp over the destination. On any error, unlink the temp and re-raise. The destination is never half-written.

purpose: Minimal HTTP server in Go's standard library
explanation: net/http is in the standard library; no framework needed for basic HTTP. HandleFunc registers a handler for a path on the default mux. ListenAndServe binds port 8080 and serves requests with the default mux. Production servers add routers (chi, gorilla/mux), middleware (logging, recovery, auth), and explicit Server values for timeouts.
walkthrough: handler matches the http.HandlerFunc signature: write to w, read from r. main registers handler on /, then blocks in ListenAndServe forever. The nil mux means use the default mux.

purpose: Validates an IPv4 address string
explanation: The regex matches four dot-separated octets, each 0..255. The octet pattern handles 250-255, 200-249, and 0-199 separately to avoid a flat \d{1,3} that would accept 999. Compiling once outside the function avoids re-parsing the regex on every call. For production, ipaddress.ip_address(s) from the standard library is more robust and handles weird inputs (leading zeros, IPv4-mapped IPv6).
walkthrough: ^ anchors at start. The group ((octet).){3} matches three octet-dot sequences. Then a final octet. $ anchors at end. The octet pattern uses three alternatives covering 250-255, 200-249, 0-199.

snippet: by_role = {role: [u for u in users if u.role == role] for role in roles}
purpose: Builds a role-keyed dict-of-lists from a flat user list
explanation: Dict comprehension: outer is keys/values, inner list comprehension filters users for each role. O(R*U) where R is roles and U is users (each user is scanned once per role). For larger inputs use a single pass with defaultdict (CE-017). Concise and pythonic for small data.
walkthrough: {role: ... for role in roles} builds the dict. The inner [u for u in users if u.role == role] filters users by role. The combined effect is a {role: [users with that role]} mapping.

purpose: Builds a vector of squares of even numbers in 1..=10
explanation: Iterator chain: range, filter, map, collect. Iterators in Rust are lazy and zero-cost — the chain fuses into a single loop after optimisation. collect()'s target type is inferred from the variable annotation; without it you'd need ::<Vec<_>>. Equivalent to Python list comprehension but compiles to nearly identical machine code as a hand-written loop.
walkthrough: 1..=10 is an inclusive range iterator. filter keeps elements where the closure returns true. map transforms each element. collect drives the chain to completion, accumulating into Vec<i32>.

snippet:
set_a, set_b = {1, 2, 3, 4}, {3, 4, 5, 6}
union = set_a | set_b
intersection = set_a & set_b
difference = set_a - set_b
symmetric = set_a ^ set_b
purpose: Set algebra in Python: union, intersection, difference, symmetric difference
explanation: Python sets are hash-based: O(1) average for membership and add/remove. The operators | & - ^ correspond to math notation. Symmetric difference is elements in either set but not both. Use cases: deduplication, fast membership tests, set algebra in graph algorithms, finding adds/removes between two snapshots.
walkthrough: | union: every element from either set. & intersection: only elements in both. - difference: elements in left but not right. ^ symmetric difference: elements in exactly one of the two sets.

purpose: Minimal Flask REST endpoint with type-converted path parameter
explanation: Flask's `<int:user_id>` converter parses the URL segment as int and rejects non-int values with a 404. jsonify wraps the dict as a JSON response with the right Content-Type. debug=True enables auto-reload + interactive tracebacks (never use in production — it allows arbitrary code execution via the debugger console).

purpose: FastAPI POST endpoint with Pydantic validation
explanation: Pydantic models validate the request body against a typed schema; if email is missing or types are wrong, FastAPI returns a 422 with a structured error. The endpoint receives a fully typed User instance. FastAPI auto-generates OpenAPI docs from the type hints. Performance: as fast as Node-equivalents because Pydantic v2 validators are written in Rust.

purpose: Express POST endpoint with JSON body parsing and validation
explanation: express.json() middleware parses JSON request bodies into req.body. Destructuring + truthiness check is the minimal validation; for richer schemas use Joi, Yup, or Zod. Status codes: 201 for created, 400 for client errors. .listen binds the port and starts the server.

purpose: Go HTTP handler with struct-tag-driven JSON decoding
explanation: Struct tags on User control how json.Decoder maps fields. Decode reads the request body and populates the struct; on parse error, return 400. Encode writes the struct as JSON. Set the Content-Type header before writing the body. For larger services, use chi or gin instead of net/http directly.

snippet:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, Column, Integer, String
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base, sessionmaker

Base = declarative_base()
class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'users'
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    name = Column(String, nullable=False)

engine = create_engine('sqlite:///app.db')
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
Session = sessionmaker(bind=engine)
with Session() as session:
    session.add(User(name='Alice'))
    session.commit()
purpose: SQLAlchemy ORM: declare schema, create tables, insert a row
explanation: declarative_base gives you a base class that maps subclasses to tables via class attributes. create_all issues CREATE TABLE for any tables not yet present. The Session is a unit of work; commit flushes pending changes. The `with` block manages session lifetime cleanly. Use Session.begin() for explicit transactions; SQLAlchemy auto-begins one on first use.

snippet:
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect('app.db')
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute('SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE active = ?', (1,))
for row in cur.fetchall():
    print(row)
conn.close()
purpose: Raw SQL via sqlite3 with parameterised query
explanation: Parameter substitution via `?` placeholders prevents SQL injection — never f-string or % into the query text. fetchall returns all rows; for large results use the cursor as an iterator (`for row in cur:`) to stream. Always close the connection (or use it as a context manager).

purpose: PostgreSQL parameterised query via node-postgres connection pool
explanation: Pool reuses connections across queries — much faster than opening a new connection per request. `$1` is the PG-style positional parameter; the second array argument supplies values, escaped by the driver. r.rows is the result array. Always use parameter binding; never interpolate user input into the SQL string.

purpose: pytest fixtures + parametrised tests
explanation: Fixtures are functions decorated with @pytest.fixture; tests opt in by naming them as parameters. parametrize generates multiple test cases from the same function, each appearing in the test report independently. Failure messages include the parameter values, so debugging is precise. Replace setUp/tearDown unittest patterns with fixtures + scope='function'/'session'.

purpose: Jest test with table-driven test.each
explanation: test() defines a single test case with a name and a body that uses expect assertions. test.each takes a 2D array of cases and a name template (with %i / %s / %p placeholders). Each row becomes its own test in the report. Jest auto-discovers files matching *.test.js / *.spec.js.

purpose: Go table-driven test in the standard library testing framework
explanation: testing.T is passed to every Test* function. The struct slice + range loop is the canonical Go table-driven pattern; each case is one assertion. t.Errorf records a failure but continues running cases; t.Fatalf would stop the test. Run with `go test`. Subtests via t.Run('name', ...) give individual case names in the report.

snippet:
import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def increment():
    global counter
    with lock:
        counter += 1
purpose: Thread-safe counter using a Lock as a context manager
explanation: Without the lock, `counter += 1` is read-modify-write across multiple bytecodes; threads can interleave and lose increments. The `with lock:` block acquires on entry and releases on exit, even on exception. Python's GIL doesn't save you here — the GIL switches mid-statement. For pure counters, threading.atomic counters (in newer pythons) or queue.Queue are alternatives.

purpose: Mutex-protected counter in Go
explanation: sync.Mutex provides Lock/Unlock. defer Unlock guarantees release even if the function panics. counter++ is now serialized across goroutines. Alternative for atomic counters: sync/atomic.AddInt64. RWMutex (sync.RWMutex) allows many readers OR one writer, useful when reads dominate.

snippet:
import threading

semaphore = threading.Semaphore(3)

def download(url):
    with semaphore:
        # only 3 downloads run concurrently
        do_download(url)
purpose: Semaphore to bound concurrency
explanation: Semaphore(3) lets up to 3 threads through at once. A Semaphore is essentially a counter: acquire decrements (blocking if zero), release increments. Useful for rate-limiting downstream calls (DB connections, third-party APIs, file handles). For asyncio, use asyncio.Semaphore. For Lock semantics with N=1, just use a Lock.

purpose: Rust thread-safe counter with Arc + Mutex
explanation: Arc (Atomically Reference-Counted) lets multiple threads own the same value; Mutex provides exclusive access. lock() returns Result; .unwrap() panics on poisoned lock. The deref `*c.lock()...` unwraps the MutexGuard. join waits for each thread. Cleaner than C++/Python equivalents because the borrow checker forces you to acknowledge sharing.

purpose: Tiny finite state machine driven by a transition table
explanation: Keys are (current_state, event), values are next_state. Compact, readable, easy to extend. For richer needs (entry/exit actions, hierarchical states, guards), use the `transitions` library. The pattern shines when the state graph is large enough to be confusing as nested if/elif but small enough to keep in one table.

snippet:
def union_find_find(parent, x):
    while parent[x] != x:
        parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]  # path compression
        x = parent[x]
    return x

def union_find_union(parent, rank, x, y):
    rx, ry = union_find_find(parent, x), union_find_find(parent, y)
    if rx == ry: return
    if rank[rx] < rank[ry]: rx, ry = ry, rx
    parent[ry] = rx
    if rank[rx] == rank[ry]: rank[rx] += 1
purpose: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) with path compression and union by rank
explanation: find returns the representative of x's set, flattening the tree along the way (path compression). union merges two sets, attaching the shorter tree under the taller (union by rank). Both operations have nearly-O(1) amortised complexity (technically O(α(n)), the inverse Ackermann function). Used in Kruskal's MST, connected-components, image segmentation, equivalence-class problems.

purpose: Knuth-Morris-Pratt string search
explanation: Builds a failure table that, when a mismatch occurs at position k in the pattern, tells you how far to slide the pattern without re-scanning text. Result: O(n + m) total time, where n is text length and m is pattern length. The naive search is O(n*m). Foundation of many string algorithms; modern equivalents (Boyer-Moore, Aho-Corasick) extend the same idea.

purpose: Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm with a binary heap
explanation: Pops the smallest-distance node, relaxes its outgoing edges, pushes updated targets. The 'if d > dist[u]: continue' check skips stale heap entries (we lazy-delete by inserting new ones). O((V + E) log V) with binary heap. Requires non-negative edge weights; for negative weights use Bellman-Ford. For dense graphs, the array variant (no heap) is O(V^2) and faster in constant.

snippet:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

for f in *.log; do
    [[ -f $f ]] || continue
    grep ERROR "$f" || true
done
purpose: Bash script that greps ERROR from every .log file, robust to no-match
explanation: set -euo pipefail makes bash actually safe: -e exit on any error, -u error on unset vars, -o pipefail propagates pipe failures. The `[[ -f $f ]] || continue` skips when the glob doesn't match (which leaves $f as the literal '*.log'). `|| true` prevents grep's exit code 1 (no match) from killing the script under -e.

snippet:
#!/bin/bash
set -e
image="myapp:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)"
docker build -t "$image" .
docker push "$image"
kubectl set image deployment/myapp app="$image"
purpose: Build, push, and deploy a Docker image tagged by git commit
explanation: Tags the image with the short SHA so each build has a unique, reproducible identifier (no 'latest' confusion). `set -e` aborts on any error; you don't want to push if the build fails or update the deployment if the push fails. kubectl set image triggers a rolling update.

purpose: Abstract Base Class defining a Storage interface
explanation: ABC + @abstractmethod enforces that subclasses implement the interface. Instantiating Storage() directly raises TypeError; only concrete subclasses (those that implement all abstract methods) can be constructed. Useful for plugin systems, dependency injection, contract definitions. typing.Protocol (PEP 544) provides structural typing without inheritance — choose ABC for nominal typing, Protocol for duck-typed interfaces.

purpose: Generator yielding sliding windows of size n over an iterable
explanation: deque with maxlen automatically drops old elements when full. The generator yields each full window as a tuple. Lazy: only one window in memory regardless of input size. itertools recipes have a similar `sliding_window` since Python 3.10 (`itertools.pairwise` is the n=2 case). Common in time-series moving averages, sequence preprocessing, n-gram extraction.

snippet:
from contextlib import suppress

with suppress(FileNotFoundError):
    os.remove('/tmp/maybe-here.txt')
purpose: Suppress a specific exception in a block without try/except
explanation: contextlib.suppress catches and ignores the named exception type(s) inside its block. Cleaner than `try: ...; except FileNotFoundError: pass` when the block is short. Be conservative — suppressing exceptions hides bugs. Multiple types: `suppress(FileNotFoundError, PermissionError)`.

purpose: Higher-order function returning a closure that captures n
explanation: `impl Fn(i32) -> bool` is the unboxed return-type-impl-trait syntax (since Rust 1.26). `move` forces the closure to take ownership of n. The returned closure can be called like a regular function. For dynamically-sized closures stored in collections, use `Box<dyn Fn(i32) -> bool>`.

purpose: Merge k sorted lists into one sorted output
explanation: Min-heap of size k holding the next candidate from each list. On each pop, advance the source list's pointer and push its next element. O(N log k) total where N is the total elements; beats merging pairwise (O(N k)). The (val, list_idx, elem_idx) tuple ensures stable ordering on ties — list_idx breaks the tie.

purpose: Length of longest strictly increasing subsequence in O(n log n)
explanation: tails[i] holds the smallest possible tail value of an LIS of length i+1 seen so far. For each new x, find where it fits via binary search; either extend (if larger than all tails) or replace the first tail >= x. Doesn't reconstruct the actual subsequence — for that, track parent pointers. The naive DP is O(n^2).

purpose: Generator function producing an infinite Fibonacci stream
explanation: function* declares a generator. yield pauses the function, returning the value to the caller; .next() resumes it. State (a, b) is preserved across calls. Infinite streams are safe because they're lazy — only the values you ask for are computed. Generators are the foundation of async/await; an async function is a generator that yields promises.

purpose: Object.freeze creates a shallow-immutable object
explanation: Object.freeze makes existing top-level properties non-writable and non-configurable. Attempts to mutate fail silently in sloppy mode, throw in strict mode. Shallow only: nested objects can still be mutated. For deep immutability use Object.freeze recursively, or a library like Immutable.js. TypeScript's `as const` is a compile-time analogue.

purpose: Auto-derive standard traits for a struct
explanation: #[derive(...)] generates implementations of common traits. Debug enables {:?} formatting, Clone enables .clone(), PartialEq enables ==. All work because each field type also implements them (f64 does). Eq, Hash, Ord, Default, Copy are other common derives. Custom logic requires manual impl. Macro hygiene + compile-time generation: zero cost at runtime.

snippet:
import asyncio

async def producer(q):
    for i in range(5):
        await q.put(i)
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    await q.put(None)  # sentinel

async def consumer(q):
    while True:
        item = await q.get()
        if item is None:
            break
        print(f'got {item}')

async def main():
    q = asyncio.Queue()
    await asyncio.gather(producer(q), consumer(q))

asyncio.run(main())
purpose: Async producer/consumer using asyncio.Queue
explanation: asyncio.Queue is the async-safe analogue of queue.Queue. put and get are coroutines. The None sentinel signals end-of-stream to the consumer. asyncio.gather runs both coroutines concurrently on the same event loop. For backpressure, asyncio.Queue accepts a maxsize; put blocks when full.

snippet:
import logging
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format='%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s',
)
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
log.info('app starting on port %d', 8000)
log.warning('low disk: %.1f GB free', 0.5)
log.exception('failed: %s', 'reason')  # call this inside except
purpose: Standard library logging setup
explanation: basicConfig configures the root logger; subsequent getLogger calls use it. Use lazy %-formatting (`'%s', x` rather than f-strings) so the args are only formatted if the level filters in. log.exception logs at ERROR with a stack trace; only meaningful inside an except block. For production, write JSON via structlog or log to a file with RotatingFileHandler.

purpose: Recursively find Python files containing TODO, excluding test directories
explanation: pathlib's Path is the modern way to handle filesystem paths. rglob is recursive glob. .parts splits the path into components for filtering. read_text reads the whole file; for huge files use open + iterate. The pattern is cleaner than os.walk + os.path.join + manual filtering.

snippet:
import subprocess

result = subprocess.run(
    ['git', 'log', '--oneline', '-n', '5'],
    capture_output=True,
    text=True,
    check=True,
)
for line in result.stdout.splitlines():
    print(line)
purpose: Run a subprocess and capture its stdout
explanation: subprocess.run is the high-level interface. Pass argv as a list (not a string) to avoid shell injection. capture_output=True captures both stdout + stderr. text=True decodes as UTF-8 (else bytes). check=True raises CalledProcessError on non-zero exit. For streaming output, use Popen + .stdout iteration.

purpose: Reduce a list to its product using functools.reduce
explanation: reduce applies a binary function cumulatively across the iterable, starting from an initial value. mul is operator.mul = lambda a, b: a*b. The initial 1 is the multiplicative identity, ensuring product([]) = 1. Python 3.8+ has math.prod which is faster and clearer for this specific use. reduce is general; prod is special-purpose.

snippet:
from itertools import groupby

rows = [
    {'team': 'A', 'name': 'Alice'},
    {'team': 'A', 'name': 'Bob'},
    {'team': 'B', 'name': 'Carol'},
]
rows.sort(key=lambda r: r['team'])
for team, group in groupby(rows, key=lambda r: r['team']):
    names = [r['name'] for r in group]
    print(team, names)
purpose: itertools.groupby clusters consecutive equal-key items
explanation: Critical caveat: groupby only groups CONSECUTIVE matches, so you must sort first by the same key. The output is (key, iterator) pairs; the iterator is single-pass (consume it before the next iteration). Same shape as SQL GROUP BY conceptually but applied to in-memory iterables.

purpose: Custom exceptions with structured fields and exception chaining
explanation: Subclass Exception (or a more specific built-in) to define custom errors. Storing host/port as attributes lets callers inspect them programmatically. `raise X from Y` sets __cause__ and prints both tracebacks; preserves the lower-level cause without losing the higher-level context. Use `from None` to suppress the cause chain.

purpose: Custom error type with errors.As for typed extraction
explanation: Define an error type by implementing Error() string. errors.As walks the error wrapping chain looking for the target type, populating the pointer if found. errors.Is checks for sentinel-error equality. Together these replace the older type-assertion + comparison patterns. fmt.Errorf with %w wraps an error; the wrapped error becomes part of the chain.

snippet:
import sys
x = [1, 2, 3]
print(sys.getsizeof(x))
print([sys.getsizeof(i) for i in x])
purpose: Inspect Python object memory size
explanation: sys.getsizeof returns the bytes used by the object, NOT including any objects it references. So a list's size includes its overhead and pointers, not the int values. For deep size, use a recursive walk or the `pympler` library. CPython int memory is ~28 bytes per number, much more than C int. NumPy arrays pack values densely.

snippet:
import cProfile, pstats

def expensive():
    return sum(i*i for i in range(1_000_000))

with cProfile.Profile() as pr:
    expensive()
stats = pstats.Stats(pr).sort_stats('cumulative')
stats.print_stats(10)
purpose: Profile a function with cProfile
explanation: cProfile records every function call, arg counts, time. Sort by cumulative time to find the heavy hitters. For line-level profiling, use line_profiler. For sampling profilers (lower overhead, runs in production), py-spy or scalene. Never optimise without profiling — your guess about where time is spent is usually wrong.

purpose: Browser Performance API timing
explanation: performance.mark stamps a named time, performance.measure computes the duration between two marks. Available in browsers and Node. Sub-millisecond precision (0.5ms in browsers, microseconds in Node). For single-shot timings, performance.now() is enough. The PerformanceObserver pattern lets you collect entries without polling.
